newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week-Base rate outlook main feature.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week-Base rate outlook main feature.

text.p: The outlook for official UK interest rates at the June 6 meeting of the Bank of England's new monetary policy committee will preoccupy UK gilt investors this week, analysts said on Tuesday.

While June short sterling has priced in a 25 basis point rise, many economists believe the Bank's interim policy committee is likely to hold off raising rates until it has a better sense of the Labour government's interim budget.
"There is the biggest chance of a wait and see approach until the Bank of England has seen the contents of the forthcoming mini-budget," said Morgan Stanley economist Mark Miller.

The budget, which Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown promised to unveil within two months of taking office, is now widely expected to be delayed until at least late June, although the Treasury has not given any indication of a date.
Continuing uncertainty over the membership of the Bank's new policy-setting committee also makes an early rate rise less likely.

"I doubt they will move rates. They have the opportunity to do so every month and it is clear that they want rates to rise gradually but persistently through the year," said Brian Hilliard, chief economist at Societe Generale.
"They may wish to wait until they have the final membership of the full committee."
Questions about who would ultimately be appointed undermined gilts last week and could remain a negative factor, he added. "The sooner that is resolved the better."
Not everyone felt the Bank would play wait and see, with some expecting a more pre-emptive monetary stance in line with its May 13 inflation report calling for a policy tightening.
"Given that the Chancellor is being slow with his budget, I think they'll say 'Well this is what we said (in the latest report),'" said NatWest Markets UK economist Geoff Dicks.
He thinks a rate rise is likely but adds: "It's a very close call."
Despite the uncertainty about next week, analysts said the main question about interest rates is when, rather than if, they will rise.

"The economic case for raising rates is fairly good, but the uncertainty is a tactical call whether a rate hike would do long term benefit or not to the status of the newly independent bank," said Salomon Brothers economist Michael Saunders.

Aside from Bank watching, gilt investors will eye Thursday's UK trade data. The overall trade deficit in March is forecast at 900 million stg versus 758 million previously. The non-EU April deficit is expected to be 600 million stg compared to 606 million in March.
Sterling's continued strength was not likely to filter through to the data significantly, analysts said.
"It is too early to see the effects of sterling's rise really. So if the trade gap is going to become a problem later on, we won't see it yet," Saunders said.
Hilliard said the trade deficit remained markedly lower than at the same point in previous cycles.
But Dharshini David, economist at HSBC Markets, said that increasing signs of UK exporters hurting from sterling could gradually shift the emphasis from monetary to fiscal tightening.

"The last thing manufacturers need is a rise in interest rates, so that could perhaps make a fiscal tightening more likely than a monetary one. Rates could go up perhaps less than initially envisioned," David said.
